hook: Billions of moths cross 600 miles of Australia using the stars.

sections.voiceover: Billions of moths cross 600 miles of Australia using the stars.
sections.visual_cue: Macro shot of a Bogong moth resting on a rock surface.

sections.voiceover: Every spring, these insects emerge from the soil across Queensland and Victoria. How do they navigate such a vast distance?
sections.visual_cue: Map showing the migration route from Queensland and Victoria to the Australian Alps.

sections.voiceover: These Bogong moths navigate their 600-mile journey using more than just the night stars.
sections.visual_cue: Close-up of a moth's antenna against a starry night sky background.

sections.voiceover: Research in Nature confirms they use a light-dependent geomagnetic inclination compass to find caves. National Geographic writer Elizabeth Landau reports this dual-system navigation guides moths across 1,000 kilometers.
sections.visual_cue: Animated diagram showing magnetic field lines and stars guiding a moth's flight path.

sections.voiceover: Nature confirms this biannual migration covers 1,000 kilometers to reach the Australian Alps.
sections.visual_cue: Wide shot of the Australian Alps at dawn.
